title: The way of not-knowing
hook: Orthodox and mystics say what God is not, since God is beyond every idea

segments.voice: Yesterday, four senses: what happened, what to believe, what to do, and where it leads. Your line was layers of meaning. Where did you find a second layer? Day one thousand sixty-eight.

The mountain is wrapped in smoke and cloud, and the ground shakes with thunder. The people at the bottom have had enough. They step back. They want Moses to speak to them instead of God. And then Exodus gives one quiet sentence: "And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Not into a blaze of light. Into the dark. Some Christians have read that sentence as a map for prayer: the closer you come to God, the less you can see. Today's word: apophatic.

Apophatic is usually explained from a Greek word for saying no. The apophatic way speaks of God by saying what God is not. God is not a thing among other things. Not made. Not in one place. Not limited. Not the size of any idea we have. Each not clears away a picture that was too small. It has a partner, the cataphatic way, which says what God is: good, light, love. Orthodox teaching holds the two together, and gives the not-saying a place of honor. Mystics in the West walked the same road. The Bible keeps both ways in view. God tells Moses, "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live." And a letter to Timothy speaks of God "dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see." Light so bright it works like darkness. Gregory of Nyssa, writing about the life of Moses, noticed the order of the story: Moses meets God first in light, at the burning bush, later in cloud, and at last in thick darkness. For Gregory, going deeper meant seeing less, and knowing more. In medieval England, an unknown writer made a small book of it, The Cloud of Unknowing. Its counsel, put simply: you won't reach God by thinking harder; reach into the cloud with love. None of this is the same as knowing nothing. It's a way of keeping God larger than your best idea, and of letting silence say what words can't.

Here's the practice: say what God is not. Settle, and breathe. Whatever you believe, try it as an exercise. On each out-breath, set down one picture that's too small. Not an old man on a cloud. Not a vending machine. Not my worst fear. Not my best idea, either. Let each one go as you breathe out. When you run out of pictures, stop, and just sit in the space that's left. Don't fill it. If you pray, you can let that empty space be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Apophatic. The way of not-knowing: speaking of God by saying what God is not, because God is beyond every idea.
Your line: more than you think. Today, when you catch yourself sure you've got someone figured out, a friend, a stranger, yourself, add a quiet not quite. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians speak of God both by what God is and, with special honor, by what God is not; in the West, contemplative Christians practice a similar wordless prayer, drawing on books like The Cloud of Unknowing.

fork.setup: you're at the foot of Sinai. the mountain is wrapped in smoke and thick darkness, and the people are stepping back in fear. you're Moses. what do you do?
options: step back with the people and wait for it to clear.
draw near to the thick darkness where God is.
climb only once the cloud has lifted.
fork.reveal: "Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Gregory of Nyssa read it as the deepest stage: going further in meant seeing less.

original.note: Greek: usually explained as a denial, a saying no; the root of apophatic.

what a scholar hears: Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses reads Moses' path as light, then cloud, then darkness: the deeper in, the less you see.

notes: Audit (fresh reviewer): all KJV/BCP quotations checked word for word, attributions and framing checked; no change needed.
'Apophatic is usually explained from a Greek word for saying no' and the original ἀπόφασις are etymology, attributed. Confirm.
Hook compresses Exodus 20:18–21 (thunder, smoke, the people asking Moses to speak to them). 'The ground shakes' draws on Exodus 19:18 (the mount quaked); confirm.
Gregory of Nyssa's light/cloud/darkness sequence (Life of Moses II.162–164) is paraphrased; confirm.
The Cloud of Unknowing paraphrased ('reach into the cloud with love'), its author called unknown and placed in medieval England with no date. Confirm.
'Orthodox Christians hold the two together, and give the not-saying a place of honor' – confirm this is a fair summary for an Orthodox reviewer.
